title: Polonnaruwa (1968)
hook: before the great stone Buddhas in Sri Lanka he describes a clarity he'd long sought

segments.voice: Yesterday, solitude is not escape: being alone for love of others. Your line was alone, for them. Who did you carry in your quiet minute? Today, Merton's long journey takes him far from Kentucky. Day two hundred eighty-six.

Autumn 1968. After twenty-seven years as a monk, Thomas Merton is given leave for a long journey abroad. He flies to Asia: Bangkok, then India, up into the Himalayan foothills, where he meets the Dalai Lama three times and they talk about prayer and meditation. Then, in early December, Sri Lanka. He visits an ancient ruined city called Polonnaruwa, where huge figures of the Buddha are carved straight into a wall of granite. He takes off his shoes and walks up to them across the wet grass. And something happens there that, he'll write, makes his whole Asian journey come clear. Today: Polonnaruwa.
screen: `AUTUMN 1968: ASIA.` → `THE DALAI LAMA, THREE TIMES.` → `BAREFOOT BEFORE THE STONE.`

segments.voice: First, the place. Polonnaruwa was a royal capital of Sri Lanka about nine hundred years ago. At a site called Gal Vihara, craftsmen cut enormous figures out of a single granite outcrop: the Buddha seated in meditation, a tall standing figure, and the Buddha lying on his side, at peace. They're still there, weathered, calm, open to the sky. Second, what Merton saw. In his journal, published after his death as The Asian Journal, he wrote that, looking at those faces, he was suddenly jerked out of his habitual way of seeing. Everything became clear, and obvious, and simple. The rock, the figures, the sky, all of it. He wrote that he felt he'd seen what he'd been obscurely looking for all his life. Third, what it wasn't. Merton didn't become a Buddhist. He was a Catholic monk on that grass, and he died one, just over a week later. He was grateful to the Buddhist tradition for the beauty and the stillness of that place, and he received the moment as a gift. Buddhists and Catholics would each describe that clarity in their own words, and it's worth not blurring them. Fourth, the Catholic thread. Scripture talks about seeing, too. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the clean of heart: for they shall see God." And Paul says: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." For Merton, Polonnaruwa was a glimpse through the glass: a moment of clean-hearted seeing, the kind of seeing contemplation had been preparing him for since that first mosaic in Rome.
screen: `GAL VIHARA: BUDDHAS IN GRANITE.` · `JERKED OUT OF HIS USUAL SEEING.` · `STILL A CATHOLIC MONK.` · `THROUGH A GLASS, THEN FACE TO FACE.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE CLEAN OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at something beautiful, for a long time. Choose one thing: a tree outside, a photo of someone you love, the grain of a table, your own hand. Look at it and keep looking, past the point where you'd usually move on. Notice when your eyes want to leave, and bring them back. Let it be exactly what it is. No commentary. If you pray, let the looking be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Polonnaruwa. The ancient city in Sri Lanka where, before the great stone Buddhas, Merton described a clarity he'd long been looking for. Today's word.
Your line: seeing clearly. Today, stop once in front of something you pass every day, and actually look at it, as if for the first time. Day two hundred eighty-six.

howItsDone: Catholic contemplatives speak of a simple, loving gaze in prayer, and many Catholics practice it by looking long at an icon, a crucifix, the Blessed Sacrament or creation.

fork.setup: you're a Catholic monk standing barefoot before great stone figures of the Buddha, and everything suddenly becomes clear. what do you do with it?
options: leave your monastery and your faith
receive it as a gift and write it down honestly
ignore it; it's not your tradition
fork.reveal: Merton wrote it down in his journal, saying his whole Asian journey had come clear, and remained a Catholic monk.

trapdoor: what you thought: Merton had a Buddhist conversion.
what it means: a Catholic monk, grateful to another tradition, described a moment of clear seeing he'd long sought.
what a scholar hears: The Asian Journal (1973), the Gal Vihara figures of the twelfth century, and readers who debate how Merton himself understood the moment.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: fixed "for the first time in twenty-seven years ... a long trip outside his monastery" (Merton had already travelled, e.g. New York 1964, California, New Mexico and Alaska in 1968); now "after twenty-seven years as a monk ... a long journey abroad". "Clearest moment of his journey" reworded to his own sense that the Asian journey had come clear; "half-seeing" (not his phrase; he wrote of a habitual, half-tied vision) changed to "his habitual way of seeing".
Douay-Rheims Matthew 5:8 and 1 Corinthians 13:12 given from memory; confirm.
Merton's Asian trip left 15 October 1968; three meetings with the Dalai Lama in Dharamsala in November; Polonnaruwa visit around 2 December 1968. Confirm dates.
Asian Journal passage is paraphrased (copyrighted), including 'jerked out of his usual half-seeing', which is close to Merton's own phrasing; confirm or rephrase.
Gal Vihara figures dated to the 12th century (Parakramabahu I); 'about nine hundred years ago' is approximate. The standing figure's identity is debated; not named.
Care taken: no suggestion that one tradition completes another; Merton remained a Catholic monk. A Keeper should check the tone. The hook's itinerary (Bangkok first, then India) should be confirmed.
